tools.name: Frying pan (about 24 cm)
tools.note: Everything happens here, in three passes.

tools.name: Spatula
tools.note: For pressing the rice flat, not just stirring.

tools.name: Kitchen scissors
tools.note: Cut the kimchi in a bowl, and the bacon too if you use it. Much faster than a knife.

tools.name: Knife
tools.note: The onion needs to be cut small.

tools.name: Cutting board
tools.note: A clean plate can stand in.

tools.name: Microwave
tools.note: For the packed rice. 2 minutes at 500 to 600 W.

tools.name: Plate
tools.note: To park the cooked seafood or bacon while the kimchi fries.

tools.name: Small bowl
tools.note: For holding the cut kimchi and its juice.

steps.title: Snip the kimchi and dice the onion
steps.text: Put the kimchi in a small bowl with its juice and snip it into bite-size pieces with kitchen scissors. Cut the onion into pieces about 5 mm across, roughly the size of the shrimp in the mix.
steps.hint: The juice is seasoning. Keep about a tablespoon of it in the bowl. Anything cut bigger than 5 mm will still be crunchy when the rice is done.

steps.title: Microwave the rice for 2 minutes
steps.text: Heat the pack, then open it and let the steam escape while you cook. Slightly dry rice fries better than fresh, moist rice.

steps.title: Cook the seafood or bacon first and take it out
steps.text: For seafood, melt 1 tbsp of butter over medium-high heat, add the mix straight from frozen, and cook for 3 minutes until the shrimp turn opaque. For bacon, skip the butter, snip it into 1 cm strips, and fry for 3 minutes until the edges crisp. Either way, move it to a plate and leave what it left behind in the pan.
steps.hint: This is the step that decides whether the fried rice is soggy. Frozen seafood dumps a lot of water, and the kimchi juice will add more, so get this water out of the pan first. Bacon leaves fat rather than water, which is worth keeping.

steps.title: Boil off the liquid, then fry the onion and kimchi
steps.text: After seafood, let the liquid in the pan bubble away for about a minute until the pan is nearly dry. After bacon, the rendered fat is ready as it is. Add the remaining 1/2 tbsp of butter, holding it back if the bacon left plenty of fat, then the onion and the garlic if using, and fry for 2 minutes until the onion turns translucent. Add the kimchi, its juice, and the sugar, and fry 2 minutes more.
steps.hint: Frying the kimchi properly is the whole recipe. Raw kimchi tastes sharp; fried kimchi turns savory and mellow. Keep the heat at medium once the butter goes in, since butter burns and turns bitter over high heat.

steps.title: Add the rice and press it flat
steps.text: If you're using the egg, push everything to one side, crack it into the bare half of the pan, and scramble it loosely for 20 seconds. Add the rice, break up the lumps, and mix until every grain is evenly colored. Then press it flat with the spatula and leave it for a minute so the bottom toasts. Turn it over and press again.
steps.hint: Pressing, not constant stirring, is what makes the crispy bits. Add the rice while the egg is still wet and it will coat the grains instead of forming lumps.

steps.title: Season at the edge and fold it back in
steps.text: Pour the soy sauce onto the bare metal around the edge so it scorches for a second, then stir it through. Return the seafood or bacon, season with salt and pepper, and toss for 30 seconds. Kill the heat, stir in the sesame oil if you have it, and scatter over the scallion or sesame. Serve straight away.
steps.hint: It only goes back at the end. Squid fried twice turns rubbery, and bacon loses its crisp edge if it sits in the rice.

troubleshooting.solution: The seafood liquid stayed in the pan, there was too much kimchi juice, or the rice was still steaming. Press the rice flat over medium heat for an extra minute or two per side to drive the moisture off.
The kimchi was very ripe and needed more frying. Add another pinch of sugar and fry 2 minutes longer. Sourness mellows with heat.
It cooked too long. Three minutes in the first pass and 30 seconds at the end is the whole budget.
Break the lumps with the edge of the spatula rather than folding them. A little extra butter helps the grains separate.
Young kimchi has less to give. Add another 1/2 tsp of soy sauce scorched at the edge of the pan, and be generous with the black pepper. Butter needs more salt than oil does.

Thin-sliced pork belly, sausage, or canned tuna all work. Fry pork or sausage in the same slot; for tuna, drain it well and add it with the rice rather than frying it first. The rice is fine with no meat at all if the kimchi is good.
